plate_findings.evidence: well-defined, homogeneous, fat-attenuation mass centered in the pancreatic head

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of pancreatic head shows homogeneous fat-attenuation encapsulated mass. Article title confirms final diagnosis is large pancreatic lipoma initially misdiagnosed as liposarcoma; liposarcoma is only initial differential, so attribution is lipoma. Pancreatic location and large size is variant presentation. B: Coronal contrast-enhanced CT of same pancreatic head fat-attenuation mass with mass effect. Same as left panel: final diagnosis per title is pancreatic lipoma, liposarcoma only misdiagnosis/differential. Variant due to rare pancreatic site and large 120x75mm size.
panels.attribution_text: Mohammadzadeh et al. Diagnostic dilemma: a large pancreatic lipoma initially misdiagnosed as liposarcoma on CT imaging.. BJR case reports 2026. doi:10.1093/bjrcr/uaag013. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced axial and coronal CT images of a 60-year-old man with abdominal pain and vomiting demonstrate a well-defined, homogeneous, fat-attenuation mass centered in the pancreatic head. The lesion is most suspicious for a liposarcoma, supported primarily by its large size, which is a typical feature of well-differentiated liposarcomas. However, the imaging features including homogeneous macroscopic fat composition, lack of internal soft tissue nodules or post-contrast enhancement, and smooth interface with the pancreatic parenchyma are compatible with both pancreatic lipoma and well differentiated liposarcoma. Yellow arrows denote the sharply marginated, encapsulated fat-density mass in the pancreatic head. The blue arrow indicates the pancreas. The green arrow shows adjacent small-bowel loops displaced by mass effect.
in_text_mentions: For further evaluation, the patient underwent a contrast-enhanced CT examination. The CT revealed a well-defined, lipid-rich mass measuring 120 × 75 mm in the head of the pancreas, accompanied by mild soft tissue swelling and mild pancreatic duct dilation. There was no SMA or SMV involvement. A 15 × 15 mm cystic component was also observed within the mass. The mean HU of the mass was -140, consistent with a fat-containing lesion. There was no evidence of biliary duct dilation or lymphadenopathy during the CT examination (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: modality, demonstrating a lesion at the level of the cerebral aqueduct. Further evaluation with brain MRI allowed more detailed characterization of the lesion. It revealed a nonenhancing 1.3-cm right paramedian fat-intensity mass consistent with a lipoma in the quadrigeminal plate cistern, with extension into the aqueduct of Sylvius without causing hydrocephalus. It was hypointense on T1 fat-saturated images (Figure 1) and hyperintense on T2-weighted images (Figure 2), compressing the brainstem anteriorly and the vermis posteriorly (Figure 3). The team chose a conservative management approach.

panels.figure_caption: Preoperative radiographic evaluation. (A) Ultrasound demonstrates a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass (42.3 mm × 25.8 mm) with a prominent internal hyperechoic line (yellow arrow) followed by strong posterior acoustic shadowing, suggesting the presence of a bony component. (B) Axial CT imaging reveals an irregularly shaped, high-density ossified core (yellow arrow) within the center of the lipomatous mass. (C) Sagittal CT reconstruction clearly demonstrates the pedunculated/sessile ossification arising from and continuous with the lingual cortex of the mandibular symphysis (yellow arrow). (D) Three-dimensional (3D) CT reconstruction provides a spatial visualization of the irregular bony protuberance (yellow arrow) projecting from the inferior border of the mandible, confirming its parosteal origin.

panels.attribution_text: Burt and Huang. Imaging review of lipomatous musculoskeletal lesions.. SICOT-J 2017. doi:10.1051/sicotj/2017015. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Lipoma: 55-year-old female with multiple palpable masses in the bilateral extremities. Multiple first degree relatives had a history of similar masses. Axial T1W pre-contrast (a) and T1W FS post-gadolinium (b) images reveal multiple, encapsulated masses which follow fat signal on all the sequences.
in_text_mentions: Though these lesions are usually solitary, they can be multiple in 5–15% of patients [1, 2, 5]. Approximately 30% of these cases are hereditary in nature, a clinically distinct entity called familial multiple lipomatosis (Figure 1); inheritance is most likely polygenic [6]. Patients with the hereditary form of multiple lipomas tend to present at a younger age in the 3rd to 4th decade of life. The lipomas can be very numerous, but the presence of a capsule around the lesion distinguishes them from lipomatosis, which is described as diffuse infiltrative mature adipose tissue.

in_text_mentions: On mammography, lipoma presents as a radiolucent lesion with regular margins, surrounded by a fine radiopaque capsule. On ultrasound, lipoma is a homogeneous lesion with variable echogenicity: isoechoic, similar to subcutaneous fat, or more rarely hyperechoic, due to densely assembled adipocytes (Fig. 1). An echogenic mass with fat density on mammography is benign and does not require biopsy [6, 7].Fig. 1Spindle cell lipoma. in_text_mentions: oration of the finger under local anaesthesia using a longitudinal skin incision. There was no difficulty in excising the mass and its margins were free. The mass was excised completely and subjected to a histopathology examination. After surgery, the patient had fully recovered the motion of the finger. Grossly, the mass was 1.5 × 1.0 cm in size and was composed of fatty tissue [Figure 2]. Histological results showed that the mass was a lipoma. There was no evidence of recurrence or restriction in motion during the 36 months of postoperative follow-up and excellent range of motion [Figure 3].

The SC/PLs presented spindle-shaped cells frequently arranged in a loose and myxoid stroma interspersed by mature adipocytes of varying sizes. in_text_mentions: Referral criteria for the 61 lipomas in this study are presented in Table 3 with the majority 34/61 (56%) referred due to their size only (>5 cm). 11 cases were referred as a result of concerning features on local imaging; 5 cases due to multiple internal septae (Figure 4), 2 cases due to prominent internal vascularity, 1 case with both internal septae and internal vascularity, 1 case with heterogenous echotexture, and 2 cases which showed enhancement following intravenous Gadolinium contrast administration. The MDT radiology categorization diagnosis determined all these lesions to be benign.

in_text_mentions: n probed with closed forceps, producing a positive "pillow sign," but did not show fat on biopsy. Forceps histology showed only hyperplastic mucosa with normal surface villi and no dysplasia. This non-diagnostic result reflects a recognized limitation of superficial biopsy, which samples the mucosa rather than the deeper submucosal fat [9]. EUS demonstrated a homogeneous, hyperechoic, well-defined submucosal mass measuring 5 × 3 × 2 cm, arising from the third echolayer (submucosa) and occupying 80% of the lumen, without regional adenopathy (Figure 2), a pattern characteristic of a lipoma [10].

panels.figure_caption: Histological and immunohistochemical findings. (A) Hematoxylin and eosin staining. The inset shows a low-magnification view, demonstrating clusters of mature adipocytes. The main panel shows a higher-magnification view of the boxed area, revealing bland spindle cells (red arrowheads) within a collagenous stroma. Thick, eosinophilic “ropey” collagen bundles (black circle) are also evident. (B) CD34 immunohistochemistry. Bland spindle cells show diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for CD34.
in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination revealed bland spindle cells admixed with mature adipocytes within a collagenous stroma, including thick eosinophilic “ropey” collagen bundles (Fig. 3A). These features are characteristic of SCL. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated diffuse CD34 positivity in the spindle cells (Fig. 3B), focal S-100 positivity, and negativity for MDM2, further supporting the diagnosis of SCL.

in_text_mentions: A triple-contrast computed tomography of the chest (Figure 1) revealed a low-density, 8-cm intraluminal mass extending caudally within the SVC, originating from the brachiocephalic junction. The caval lumen was completely occluded, and this finding was confirmed by magnetic resonance angiography. A presumptive diagnosis of vascular sarcoma was made. After multidisciplinary discussion with vascular, thoracic, and cardiac surgeons, surgical resection of the mass was planned. source_variant.figure_caption: Histopathological features of the mandibular parosteal lipoma (H&E staining). (A) Low-power view (scale bar: 1 mm) showing mature adipose tissue infiltrating and compartmentalizing skeletal muscle bundles, characteristic of deep-seated lipomatous growth. (B) Intermediate magnification (100×) revealing the intimate association between mature adipocytes and reactive bone trabeculae. (C) High-power view (200×) of the osseous component; note the presence of viable osteocytes within lacunae, confirming mature, benign bone formation rather than malignant osteogenesis. (D) Higher magnification (200×) demonstrating uniform, mature adipocytes without nuclear atypia, hyperchromasia, or lipoblasts, consistent with a benign lesion.

plate_findings.evidence: hypoattenuating fatty mass in the distal interventricular septum

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial unenhanced CT in 60-year-old male shows hypoattenuating fatty mass in distal interventricular septum, characterized as intramyocardial lipoma / lipomatous mass in caption and in-text. Real patient CT with fat-attenuation lesion matching lipoma vocabulary. B: Sagittal unenhanced CT shows same intramyocardial lipomatous mass within septal wall. Article diagnosis is intramyocardial lipoma, a configured disease, not other disease; mimicked condition is post-infarction change. C: Sagittal arterial phase CT from 6 years prior shows stable lipomatous lesion in septal wall, supporting intramyocardial lipoma diagnosis. Real patient CT fat-attenuation lesion. D: Axial venous phase CT from 6 years prior shows lipomatous mass within septal wall, stable intramyocardial lipoma. Real patient CT fat-attenuation lesion.
panels.attribution_text: Wood et al. An Intramyocardial Lipoma Mimicking Post-infarction Fatty Changes: Discussion of Key Distinguishing Imaging Findings and Clinical Implications.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.46955. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Axial (A) and sagittal (B) unenhanced computed tomography revealed a hypoattenuating fatty mass in the distal interventricular septum. Sagittal arterial phase (C) and axial venous phase (D) from a CT kidney six years prior better delineate the chambers of the heart and the position of the lipomatous mass within the septal wall. Axial arterial phase images did not reveal the lesion as clearly as sagittal images. RV: right ventricle; LA: left atrium; LV: left ventricle; Ao: aorta.
in_text_mentions: A 60-year-old male with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 35-pack-year smoking history with dyspnea on exertion was referred for a screening low-dose CT chest. CT scan revealed a focal fatty-attenuating region within the distal inferoseptum, which was initially thought to be lipomatous changes concerning for prior myocardial infarction given the patient’s cardiac risk factors (Figures 1A, 1B). Upon review of prior CT studies, the lipomatous lesion had been stable for six years but had not been definitively characterized (Figures 1C, 1D).

in_text_mentions: oint movements. For further evaluation, she underwent radiological investigations including X-ray, ultrasonography, non-contrast CT, and MRI. plate_findings.evidence: hyperintense to muscle on T1WI

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (T1W, T2W, STIR, POST CONTRAST, GRE). T1W: Coronal T1W MRI panel showing well-circumscribed oval lesion abutting cortex of proximal femur, hyperintense to muscle, consistent with parosteal lipoma in lipoma article. T2W: Coronal T2W MRI panel showing same well-circumscribed oval femoral lesion hyperintense to muscle, supporting fat-signal lipoma. STIR: STIR MRI panel showing suppression of the oval femoral lesion, characteristic fat-signal behavior of lipoma. POST CONTRAST: Post-contrast MRI panel of same parosteal thigh lesion with no significant enhancement of the fatty component, consistent with lipoma. GRE: GRE MRI panel showing same well-circumscribed oval lesion abutting femoral cortex displacing thigh muscles, part of lipoma MRI series.
panels.attribution_text: Shah et al. Parosteal Lipoma of the Thigh: A Report of a Rare Case and Review of the Literature.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.99681. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: MRI findings The images show a well-circumscribed oval lesion noted abutting the cortex of the femur, appearing hyperintense to muscle on T1WI, T2WI, and suppressed on STIR. An ill-defined hypointense area noted within the lesion along the medial cortical margin of the proximal end of shaft of femur suggestive of osseous excrescences. Periosteal reaction noted along the cortical margin of the femur, with cortical thickening; however, no continuity with the medullary cavity is noted. On post-contrast, a few areas around the osseous excrescences show mild heterogeneous enhancement. The rest of the lesion shows no significant enhancement. There is no evidence of septations within the lesion. No associated solid component is observed. Additionally, there is no bone marrow edema or neurovascular invasion noted MRI: magnetic resonance imaging; STIR: short tau inversion recovery; GRE: gradient echo
in_text_mentions: 120 to -60 HU) lesion was observed on the medial aspect of the proximal thigh, near the diaphysis of the right femur, with a thick periosteal reaction and bone excrescence extending from the femur into the lesion. No communication with the medullary cavity was seen (Figure 3). Subsequently, MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed oval lesion adjacent to the anteromedial cortex of the femoral diaphysis, displacing the surrounding thigh muscles. The lesion appeared hyperintense to muscle on T1WI and T2WI and was suppressed on STIR. Post-contrast images showed no evidence of enhancement (Figure 4).

in_text_mentions: tted the femoral shaft, was predominantly hyperechoic with some heterogeneous areas, and maintained smooth borders. No internal vascularity was noted. CT scan confirmed a well-defined, homogeneous, hypodense, non-enhancing soft tissue mass located between the right femur and surrounding musculature, measuring 39 × 10 × 13.5 cm. The lesion had a density of approximately −100 Hounsfield Units, which consistent with adipose tissue, and thin internal septations without nodular enhancement and with thin non-enhancing septations and a few foci of calcification, consistent with a fatty mass (Fig. 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). B: Bottom axial CT with blue arrow shows same fat-density mass in descending colon with intussusception, described as consistent with submucosal lipoma. panels.rationale: Single preoperative clinical photo of pediatric patient with massive left scrotal enlargement. Article title establishes diagnosis as largest pediatric scrotal lipoma; caption + in-text describe the pictured swelling as 11cm soft non-tender mass due to that lipoma, mimicking hydrocele. Visible manifestation maps to subcutaneous soft lipoma nodule. Atypical due to giant size, scrotal-perineal location and rarity emphasized as expanding anatomic spectrum.
panels.attribution_text: Abdelmohsen. Largest pediatric scrotal lipoma with perineal extension: a rare case expanding the anatomic spectrum and diagnostic pitfalls.. BMC urology 2026. doi:10.1186/s12894-026-02240-z. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative appearance demonstrating marked left scrotal asymmetry with massive enlargement mimicking the typical clinical presentation of large hydrocele in a pediatric patient. Note the smooth contour and absence of erythema or other signs of acute pathology
in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed marked scrotal asymmetry with significant left hemiscrotum enlargement (Fig. 1). A large (approximately 11 cm), soft, non-tender, not reducible swelling occupied the entire left hemiscrotum extending into the inguinal region, with pseudofluctuation leading to initial clinical impression of large hydrocele rather than inguinal hernia. The left testis was difficult to palpate due to mass size; the right testis was normal.

plate_findings.evidence: well-defined retroperitoneal mass located anterior to the external iliac vessels, compressing the adjacent structures without internal enhancement

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: Coronal early-phase CT of retroperitoneal mass in article titled retroperitoneal lipoma extending into inguinal canal; captioned well-defined mass without enhancement corresponds to lipomatous lesion. B: Axial early-phase CT of same retroperitoneal lipoma mass; captioned manifestation plus disease-focused title supports lipoma attribution. C: Coronal delayed-phase CT of same retroperitoneal lipoma; no enhancement, mass effect consistent with lipoma. D: Axial delayed-phase CT of same retroperitoneal lipoma mass. E: Early-phase coronal CT showing tumor relationship to inferior epigastric vessels; same lipoma mass in lipoma case report. F: Early-phase axial CT of same retroperitoneal lipoma mass. G: Sagittal CT shows tumor prolapsing into inguinal canal, matching title retroperitoneal lipoma extending into inguinal canal; recognized less common extension so variant.
panels.attribution_text: Okuchi et al. Totally laparoscopic excision of a retroperitoneal lipoma extending into the inguinal canal: a rare case report with intraoperative video.. International journal of surgery case reports 2026. doi:10.1097/rc9.0000000000000637. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced CT findings of the pelvic mass. Coronal (A) and axial (B) images in the early phase, and coronal (C) and axial (D) images in the delayed phase show a well-defined retroperitoneal mass located anterior to the external iliac vessels, compressing the adjacent structures without internal enhancement. Early-phase coronal (E) and axial (F) images show the inferior epigastric vessels located caudal to the tumor. Yellow arrowheads and arrows, respectively, indicate the right external iliac artery and the inferior epigastric artery. White arrowheads in (G) indicate the tumor prolapsing into the inguinal canal.
